title: 3 Uniquely Powerful Ways To Praise Your Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Building on SCM's principle that praise should be reserved for genuine accomplishment, Linsin offers three understated but powerful ways to deliver it. The wordless fist bump involves letting a student privately enjoy an accomplishment before approaching calmly and holding out a fist for them to reach and bump, without further comment. The smile and nod from across the room lets a teacher silently acknowledge a student's success from a distance, particularly meaningful if the student is caught watching for the teacher's reaction. The surprise note involves writing a short, specific, heartfelt note on nice stationery, folded and delivered privately. Linsin explains that subtlety often makes praise more powerful than overt enthusiasm because it recognizes something the student is already feeling internally rather than overshadowing it, though he notes that occasional over-the-top praise still has its place in the right moment.
points: Praise should be reserved for genuine achievement or effort beyond what's normally expected, not routine behavior.
The wordless fist bump lets a student enjoy an accomplishment privately before a brief, silent acknowledgment.
A smile and nod from across the room can silently affirm a student's success without disrupting their moment.
A handwritten surprise note, kept brief and sincere, can be remembered by students for decades.
Subtle praise is often more meaningful than overt praise because it recognizes what the student is already feeling rather than overshadowing it.
quotes: There is power in acknowledging true accomplishment with the smallest, simplest gesture.
When the student knows what prompted your praise, there is no reason to say anything at all. In fact, it’s often best if you don’t.
I have former students who still have notes I wrote to them more than 20 years ago.
Because you're recognizing something the student is already feeling inside. You're not overshadowing their accomplishment or disrupting their quiet satisfaction.
Noticing improvement, hard work, or success beyond what your students have done before, and simply noting it—the pure truth of it—can be profoundly meaningful to them.
